l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: Pausanias describes the harbours, monuments, temples, walls, paintings, and myths of Attica, especially the approaches to Athens and the city’s public buildings. He recounts the roles of Themistocles, Theseus, Conon, and other Athenians, and identifies works by artists including Praxiteles, Phidias, and Euphranor. He also digresses on the Galati or Celts, their invasion of Greece, their defeat near Thermopylæ and Delphi, and their later settlement in Asia Minor. The account ends with the tribal heroes of Athens and the benefactions of Emperor Adrian.

l: Pausanias, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: Pausanias describes the places, monuments, temples, statues, paintings, traditions, and histories of Attica. He often distinguishes popular traditions from accounts based on closer inquiry.

l: Attica, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: Attica contains the promontory of Sunium, the harbours of Piraeus, Munychia, and Phalerum, and the city of Athens. It was formerly called Actæa, and the name Attica was said to derive from Atthis, the daughter of Cranaus.

l: Athenians, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: The Athenians formerly worked silver mines at Laurium and used Phalerum before Themistocles made Piraeus their principal port. They fought the Persians, Macedonians, and Galati, and sent forces to Thermopylæ against the Celtic invasion.

l: Piraeus, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: Piraeus was a township in ancient times and became a port under Themistocles. It had three harbours, ship stations, the tomb of Themistocles, temples of Athene and Zeus, paintings, porticoes, and a temple of Aphrodite erected by Conon.

l: Phalerum, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: Phalerum was the Athenians’ port before Themistocles established Piraeus, because it was nearer to Athens. Menestheus was said to have sailed from there to Troy, and the area contained temples of Artemis, Demeter, Sciradian Athene, and Zeus, as well as several altars.

l: Themistocles, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: Themistocles made Piraeus the port of Athens because it seemed more convenient and provided three harbours instead of one. The walls he built after the Persian defeat were later pulled down by the Thirty Tyrants, and a tomb of Themistocles stood at the largest harbour; his sons later returned from exile and dedicated a painting of him in the Parthenon.

l: Theseus, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: Theseus was said to have sailed from Phalerum to avenge the death of Androgeos, and traditions differed about whether he carried off Antiope or received her help in taking Themiscyra. Paintings and stories in Athens portrayed him as restoring political equality, though Pausanias rejects the popular belief that he ruled as a king followed by a line of descendants.

l: Athene, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: Temples and statues of Athene stood at Sunium, Piraeus, Phalerum, and elsewhere in Athens. In Piraeus, Athene was represented armed with a spear beside Zeus, while at Cnidus a goddess generally called Athene was called by the Cnidians Athene of the Fair Voyage.

l: Zeus, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: Zeus was worshipped in temples and represented in statues at Piraeus, Phalerum, and Athens. At Piraeus his statue was of gold and held a sceptre and Victory; in Athens he appeared as Zeus Eleutherius and Zeus the Counsellor.

l: Ceramicus, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: Ceramicus took its name from the hero Ceramus, who was reputed to be the son of Dionysus and Ariadne. Its area included the royal portico, paintings, temples, the council chamber, and the Rotunda.

l: Galati, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: The Galati came from the remotest parts of Europe and invaded Greece after overrunning Illyria, the lands between Illyria and Macedonia, Macedonia, and Thessaly. They were defeated near Delphi by the Delphians, Phocians, and Ætolians with the aid of storms, falling rocks, and heroic warriors, and many later crossed into Asia Minor.

l: Celts, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: The people later called Galati were originally called Celts by themselves and by other nations. Their army invaded Greece, reached Thermopylæ, and sought to plunder the treasures at Delphi before being driven back.

l: Thermopylæ, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: The Athenians and other Greek volunteers tried to block the Galati at Thermopylæ under Callippus. The Galati discovered the pass previously used by Ephialtes, routed the Phocians stationed there, and entered Greece, while Athenian forces suffered heavily in the muddy waters near the Lamiac Gulf.

l: Delphi, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: The Galati marched toward Delphi intending to plunder the treasures of the god. The Delphians, nearby Phocians, and an Ætolian contingent resisted them, and after the victory the Delphians offered sacrifice to Pyrrhus, whose tomb they had previously dishonoured.

l: Emperor Adrian, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: Emperor Adrian was honoured in Athens with a statue among the city’s benefactors and was described as especially beneficial to the peoples he ruled. He was said to have avoided war except when suppressing the revolt of the Hebrews, and inscriptions in the temple common to all the gods recorded his temples, gifts, and other benefactions.

l: Celtic invasion of Greece, Description of Greece, Description of Greece / BOOK I.--ATTICA.
s: The Celtic invasion brought an army through Illyria, Macedonia, and Thessaly to Thermopylæ. The invaders forced the pass by the route used by Ephialtes and then advanced toward Delphi, where Greek forces defeated them; many survivors crossed into Asia Minor and established themselves in the region later called Galatia.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The unit records the early actions of Ptolemy and the origins of his rule over Egypt, as well as the rise and fall of Antigonus. Ptolemy seized Egypt, Syria, and Phœnicia, resisted Perdiccas, formed alliances against Antigonus, and defended Egypt against invasion. Antigonus and Demetrius failed to capture Egypt and Rhodes, and Antigonus later lost his power and died. The text also discusses Ptolemy’s alleged descent from Philip and the distribution of Alexander’s empire into separate kingdoms.

l: Attalus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Attalus is mentioned among the rulers whose actions had become ancient and whose exploits had not been adequately recorded.

l: Ptolemy, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Ptolemy distinguished himself in Asia Minor and aided Alexander at Oxydracæ. After Alexander’s death, he resisted giving Alexander’s dominions to Aridæus, supported dividing the empire into separate kingdoms, seized Egypt, and killed Cleomenes. He later took Syria, Phœnicia, and Cyprus, allied with Cassander, Lysimachus, and Seleucus against Antigonus, defended Egypt from invasion, aided Rhodes, and restored Pyrrhus to Thesprotian Epirus.

l: Alexander, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Alexander was aided by Ptolemy when danger befell him at Oxydracæ. After his death, his dominions were divided into separate kingdoms, and his body was taken to Memphis and buried there with Macedonian rites.

l: Perdiccas, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Perdiccas attempted to take the kingdom of Egypt from Ptolemy while leading Aridæus and the young Alexander with him. After being driven out of Egypt, losing prestige, and becoming unpopular among the Macedonians, he was assassinated by his bodyguard.

l: Seleucus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Seleucus, the son of Antiochus, was driven into exile by Antigonus and was welcomed by Ptolemy. Ptolemy persuaded Cassander and Lysimachus to join him in opposing the exile of Seleucus and the growing power of Antigonus.

l: Antigonus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Antigonus opposed Ptolemy and seized Syria and Phœnicia while Ptolemy was in Libya, placing them under Demetrius. He later besieged Egypt by land and sea and sent Demetrius against Rhodes, but failed against both Rhodes and Egypt. He subsequently fought Lysimachus, Cassander, and Seleucus, lost most of his forces, and died.

l: Demetrius, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Demetrius, the son of Antigonus, was placed in control of Syria and Phœnicia and defeated some Egyptian forces after Ptolemy’s return. He later defeated Menelaus at Cyprus, helped blockade Ptolemy in Egypt, and besieged Rhodes with a large army and fleet, but did not succeed.

l: Macedonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The Macedonians believed that Ptolemy was really the son of Philip, although he was officially regarded as the son of Lagus. They also became hostile to Perdiccas after his failed expedition against Egypt and other grounds.

l: Egypt, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Ptolemy entered Egypt, killed Cleomenes, secured the country with garrisons, and defended it against Perdiccas, Antigonus, and Demetrius. Egypt was protected at Pelusium by land forces and by a fleet guarding the river.

l: Syria, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Ptolemy seized Syria after the death of Perdiccas, but Antigonus later took it by surprise and handed it over to Demetrius. After Antigonus’s death, Ptolemy took Syria again.

l: Phœnicia, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Ptolemy seized Phœnicia together with Syria after the death of Perdiccas. Antigonus later captured it and placed it under Demetrius, and Ptolemy subsequently recovered it after Antigonus’s death.

l: government of Egypt and of the Mysi, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The unit proposes to explain how the government of Egypt and of the Mysi, along with that of neighboring nations, came to the fathers of Ptolemy and Attalus.

l: kingdom of Egypt, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Perdiccas plotted to take the kingdom of Egypt from Ptolemy but was driven out. Ptolemy preserved the kingdom when Antigonus and Demetrius attacked it.

l: kingdoms, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: After the death of Alexander, Ptolemy was chiefly responsible for having the different nationalities divided into kingdoms.

l: war against Antigonus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Ptolemy persuaded Cassander and Lysimachus to join him in war against Antigonus, presenting the exile of Seleucus and Antigonus’s aggrandizement as a common danger. The conflict included fighting in Syria, Phœnicia, Cyprus, Egypt, and Rhodes, and ended with Antigonus losing most of his forces and dying.

l: siege of Egypt, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Antigonus and Demetrius blockaded Egypt by land and sea after Ptolemy fled there. Ptolemy maintained his position at Pelusium with an army and used his fleet to keep the enemy from the river, preventing the capture of Egypt.

l: death of Alexander, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: After the death of Alexander, Ptolemy resisted giving all of Alexander’s dominions to Aridæus and helped divide the empire into separate kingdoms. Alexander’s body was diverted from its intended burial at Ægæ and buried by Ptolemy at Memphis.

l: assassination of Perdiccas, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: Perdiccas was assassinated by his bodyguard after his failed attempt to take Egypt from Ptolemy left him without his former prestige and unpopular among the Macedonians.

l: power of Antigonus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VI.
s: The power of Antigonus was opposed by Ptolemy, Cassander, Lysimachus, and Seleucus. Antigonus eventually fought their combined forces, lost most of his army, and died, bringing about the defeat of his power.

l: Description of Greece, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: The unit describes Ptolemy I Soter’s family conflicts, his wars involving Magas of Cyrene and Antiochus I, and the succession and conduct of later Ptolemies. It recounts Attalus I’s rise, Philetærus’s revolt, Demosthenes’ exile, and the statues and historical figures commemorated by the Athenians. It traces Lysimachus’s wars, marriage to Arsinoe, conflict with Agathocles, and eventual death against Seleucus I. It then follows Pyrrhus of Epirus from his ancestry and struggles in Epirus and Macedonia to his campaigns in Italy and Sicily against the Romans and Carthaginians.

l: Ptolemy, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Ptolemy I Soter married his sister Arsinoe, killed his brother Argæus and another brother, and brought Alexander’s corpse from Memphis. He opposed Magas of Cyrene and Antiochus I, sent forces against Antigonus I, and had sons by the daughter of Lysimachus rather than by Arsinoe.

l: Alexander, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Alexander the Great’s corpse was brought from Memphis by Ptolemy I Soter. He is described as having first brought elephants to Europe after conquering Porus and India, and as being related by his mother to the Æacidæ of Epirus.

l: Magas of Cyrene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Magas, the uterine brother of Ptolemy I Soter, was appointed governor of Cyrene by his mother Berenice. He persuaded Cyrene to revolt, marched toward Egypt, and was forced to turn back when the Marmaridæ revolted; as the husband of Apame, he also persuaded Antiochus I to attack Egypt.

l: Cyrene, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Cyrene revolted from Ptolemy I Soter after Magas persuaded its people to support him. Magas marched with an army from Cyrene toward Egypt but turned back when the Marmaridæ rebelled.

l: Antiochus I, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Antiochus I was persuaded by Magas to violate the agreement made by Seleucus I with Ptolemy I Soter and prepare an invasion of Egypt. Ptolemy sent raiders into his territory and checked stronger forces, preventing the invasion.

l: Seleucus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Seleucus I had made conditions with Ptolemy I Soter that Antiochus I was persuaded to violate. He later received Lysandra, her sons and brothers, and Alexander, the son of Lysimachus, when they fled from Lysimachus.

l: Egypt, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Egypt was threatened by Magas of Cyrene and Antiochus I, but Ptolemy I Soter defended it by guarding the approaches, using troops, and sending forces to ravage Antiochus’s territory. A group of 4,000 Galati mercenaries sent to a desert island in the Nile perished there.

l: Athenians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Athenians received aid from Ptolemy I Soter against Antigonus I and later erected statues of Ptolemy VI Philometor and Berenice. They also displayed statues of historical figures including Attalus I, Demosthenes, and Lysimachus.

l: Antigonus I, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Antigonus I and the Macedonians opposed the Athenians, against whom Ptolemy I Soter sent a fleet. Lysimachus later destroyed Antigonus I’s rule in Asia Minor.

l: Macedonians, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Macedonians regarded marriage between siblings as unusual, unlike the Egyptians. They fought against the Athenians, supported Cassander and his sons, and later opposed Pyrrhus of Epirus.

l: Attalus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Attalus I, nephew of Philetærus, received the kingdom from his cousin Eumenes. His greatest stated achievement was compelling the Galati to leave the coast and settle inland in Galatia.

l: Philetærus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Philetærus, a Paphlagonian eunuch associated with Docimus, revolted from Lysimachus and invited Seleucus I. Later, indignant at Agathocles’ death and suspicious of Arsinoe, he occupied Pergamum and offered himself and Lysimachus’s money to Seleucus.

l: Demosthenes, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Demosthenes was twice driven into exile by the Athenians, first to Calauria and later again after the defeat at Lamia. He returned to Calauria and died there by taking poison; he was the only exile whom Archias did not hand over to Antipater and the Macedonians.

l: Ptolemy II Philadelphus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Ptolemy II Philadelphus was one of the Egyptian kings whose statue stood in the Athenian Odeum, and he was also represented among the Athenian Eponymi. A statue of his sister Arsinoe stood near his.

l: Ptolemy VI Philometor, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Ptolemy VI Philometor was banished to Cyprus by his father at the urging of Cleopatra I, but returned after Alexander, his younger brother, fled and his mother was killed. He regained Egypt, suppressed the revolt of the Thebans, and was honored at Athens with a bronze statue alongside Berenice.

l: Cleopatra I, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Cleopatra I disliked her eldest son Ptolemy VI Philometor and sought to have Alexander, his younger brother, chosen king. She fabricated a plot against her by mutilating eunuchs, but was eventually killed by Alexander.

l: Alexander (brother of Ptolemy VI), Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Alexander, the younger brother of Ptolemy VI Philometor, was sent to Cyprus by Cleopatra I and later became king when Philometor fled. He killed Cleopatra after she had helped secure his accession, then fled when the crime was discovered, allowing Philometor to return.

l: Philip, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Philip II of Macedon and his son Alexander were represented by statues near those of the Egyptian kings in Athens. The Athenians honored them with gifts and statues, partly from communal flattery.

l: Lysimachus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Lysimachus ruled Thracian territory after Alexander the Great’s death, fought the Odrysæ, Dromichetes, Demetrius I Poliorcetes, and Pyrrhus of Epirus, and eventually ruled Macedonia. He married Arsinoe, permitted Agathocles’ execution, was defeated by Seleucus I, and was killed in the battle.

l: Agathocles, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Agathocles, the son of Lysimachus, was captured by the Getæ during a campaign against Dromichetes. He later had children by Lysandra but was killed after Arsinoe conspired against him, causing Lysandra and others to flee to Seleucus.

l: Arsinoe (wife of Lysimachus), Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Arsinoe, the wife of Lysimachus and sister of Lysandra, was said to have feared that her children would fall under Agathocles’ control after Lysimachus’s death. She therefore conspired against Agathocles; some writers instead claimed that she had fallen violently in love with him and plotted his death after being rejected.

l: Thrace, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Lysimachus ruled the part of Thrace adjoining Macedonia after Alexander the Great’s death. The text says that Thrace was densely populated and later became subject to the Romans.

l: Epirus, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Epirus was ruled by the descendants of Pyrrhus and was involved in the succession struggles of Æacides, Alcetas, and Pyrrhus of Epirus. Lysimachus ravaged Epirus and was accused, though the account doubts it, of disturbing the tombs of its kings.

l: Demetrius, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Demetrius I Poliorcetes succeeded Antigonus I and caused Lysimachus to anticipate war. Lysimachus fought him at Amphipolis, while Pyrrhus aided Lysimachus; Demetrius later crossed into Asia Minor and was captured by Seleucus.

l: Pyrrhus, the son of Achilles, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Pyrrhus of Epirus became king after returning from exile with Egyptian aid supplied by Ptolemy I Soter. He fought in Corcyra, Macedonia, and against Lysimachus, then crossed into Italy at the invitation of Tarentum and later Sicily at the invitation of Syracuse.

l: Cassander, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Cassander and his sons maintained friendship with Lysimachus while ruling Macedonia. Cassander opposed Æacides, prevented his return to Epirus, and later marched against the young Pyrrhus.

l: Romans, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: The Romans fought Pyrrhus of Epirus in Italy and were initially thrown into confusion by his unexpected arrival and elephants. They later blockaded or attacked Tarentum, while the text says that Pyrrhus was the first Greek known to wage war against them.

l: Tarentum, Description of Greece, CHAPTER VII.
s: Tarentum invited Pyrrhus of Epirus to fight the Romans because it could not resist them alone. Its envoys appealed to Pyrrhus as a friend and suppliant people, and Tarentum had previously aided him with its fleet against Corcyra.
